Threat.value: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me

Memory.value: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop

vignette:
Matiu was 53, a veteran captain for a major airline, and had spent twenty-five years in the cockpit of long-haul aircraft. He was also a survivor of torture. During a layover in a country he no longer named, he had been detained by security forces who accused him of espionage. For three days they kept him in a concrete room, hooded, and subjected him to near-drowning and electric shocks. The interrogators spoke softly, almost politely, and the silence between their questions was the worst part—a thick, waiting quiet that he knew meant the next blow was coming. When they finally released him, he was told never to speak of it. He didn’t. He flew home, told his wife he’d had a bad stomach bug, and went back to work.

Now, four years later, Matiu could no longer ignore what was happening to him. The memory of the room returned unbidden, not as a story but as a sensory event. He would be walking through a hotel lobby or sitting in a crew briefing, and suddenly he could smell the damp concrete and his own sweat, and the image would snap into his mind with the crisp, silent clarity of a photograph. When that happened, the emotion would hit him so hard—a wave of terror and helplessness—that he would have to stop whatever he was doing, excuse himself, and lock himself in a bathroom stall until his hands stopped shaking. These olfactory and photographic intrusions were most reliably triggered by two things: crowds and people misbehaving. A crowded airport gate, with passengers jostling and ignoring instructions, would send his heart racing. But the more potent trigger was moral violation—seeing a person act rudely or cruelly, like a passenger screaming at a gate agent or a driver cutting someone off. That flash of injustice was enough to drop him back into the room.

What frightened Matiu most was the silence. Unusual silence—the quiet of an empty crew lounge, the hush in the cockpit during a long, uneventful cruise—made him feel certain that something dangerous was about to happen. His body would lock into high alert, and he would begin watching his colleagues closely, scanning their faces for signs of threat. He had come to believe that if he let his guard down, he would be caught off guard again. So he watched. He watched passengers for sudden movements, watched the flight deck door for any unexpected sound, watched the faces of the first officer and the cabin crew for flickers of hostility. He also checked his apartment door and windows three times before bed, and once more after lying down. At work, he had started avoiding crowded pre-flight briefings, arriving early to be alone in the cockpit. He told himself it was professionalism.

The cycle had tightened over the past year. A trigger—say, a passenger shouting at a flight attendant—would throw him into memory, and the memory would convince him that danger was imminent, and that conviction would make him hypervigilant, scanning every face, every shadow. That hypervigilance, in turn, made him more sensitive to triggers. He would notice a minor rudeness he might have overlooked before, and the loop would start again. He had stopped going to his daughter’s school plays because the crowded auditorium felt unbearable. His wife had begun to ask, gently, why he seemed so distant. He told her he was just tired from the long flights.

What finally brought Matiu to seek help was a moment in the cockpit. During a quiet night crossing over the Pacific, the cabin lights dimmed, the autopilot engaged, and the silence became absolute. He felt the familiar dread rise, and for the first time, he could not shake the image of the concrete room. He had to hand control to the first officer and sit with his head in his hands for ten minutes. He realized, with a cold certainty, that he could lose his license. That night, he told his wife the truth. The next day, he called a psychologist who specialized in trauma. He was terrified that talking about it would make the memories worse, but he was more afraid of what would happen if he kept them locked inside.
